overview:
Spain fills most of the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe, sharing it with Portugal and the tiny state of Andorra. Only about 14 kilometers of water separate its southern tip from Africa at the Strait of Gibraltar. Spain is roughly twice the size of Oregon and also governs the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean and the volcanic Canary Islands off the African coast. Madrid, the capital, sits almost exactly in the middle of the country on a high plateau.

About 48 million people live in Spain. Spanish, which Spaniards often call Castilian, is the national language, while Catalan, Galician and Basque are official in their own regions; Basque is related to no other known language. Spain is a constitutional monarchy, with a king as head of state and an elected parliament. It is the world's leading producer of olive oil, one of the most visited countries on Earth, and a place where life is built around late meals, long evenings and crowded public squares.
landAndNature: Spain is the second most mountainous country in Europe after Switzerland. The Pyrenees seal the border with France, the Picos de Europa rise above the green, rainy north, and the Sierra Nevada in the far south holds snow within sight of the Mediterranean. Between them spreads the Meseta, a wide plateau of wheat, vines and olive groves that bakes in summer and freezes in winter. The Canary Islands are volcanic, and Mount Teide on Tenerife is Spain's highest point at 3,715 meters. The marshes of Doñana shelter flamingos and the Iberian lynx, the world's rarest cat, brought back from the edge of extinction.
peopleAndCulture: Spanish life runs late: lunch near two, dinner after nine, and children playing in the plaza long after bedtime elsewhere. Tapas, small plates shared standing at a bar, turn eating into a social sport, and paella, jamón and tortilla de patatas are national staples. Every region guards its own festivals: the Fallas bonfires of Valencia, Seville's Easter processions and April fair, and the running of the bulls at San Fermín in Pamplona. Flamenco, with its guitar, handclaps and stamping heels, grew out of Andalusia's Roma communities. Soccer is close to a religion, and Spain won the World Cup in 2010.
history: Cave painters at Altamira left bison in red and black about 15,000 years ago. Phoenicians, Greeks, Carthaginians and then Romans settled the peninsula, followed by the Visigoths. In 711 Muslim armies crossed from North Africa and ruled much of Spain for centuries, making Córdoba one of the world's great cities of learning and leaving behind the Alhambra palace at Granada. Christian kingdoms gradually took the land back, finishing in 1492, the year Columbus sailed west for Spain. Silver from the Americas made Spain the strongest power in Europe before it slowly declined. A civil war from 1936 to 1939 brought General Franco to power as dictator until his death in 1975, after which Spain returned to democracy.
funFacts: Spain produces roughly half the world's olive oil, and some of its groves contain trees over a thousand years old.
The Sagrada Família church in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882 and is still unfinished.
Basque, spoken in northern Spain and southwestern France, is unrelated to any other known language on Earth.
La Tomatina in Buñol sends thousands of people hurling about 100 tons of ripe tomatoes at one another each August.
Spanish is the world's second most spoken native language, used by more than 400 million people as a first language.
